utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one question for clarification. When were you first assigned a pistol from the Mebos company to use as a security officer there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in November of 1991, November or December. It was a pistol that was used by many people. It went from one person to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you would turn the pistol over to the person who would come in on the next shift?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during that week that you worked from the 18th to the 24th of April, did someone always come in on the next shift?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We couldn't hear your answer. The question was: When you worked in April, between the 18th and the 24th of the month, did someone always come in on the next shift to take the gun?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What would you do if someone didn't come to take the gun, take custody of the gun?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I would lock them in the drawer and sometimes I would take it home with me when I went home for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the 24th. You go to work on April 24th, you have a conversation with your supervisor?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what happens.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They sent me home, told me they would call me when they needed me, and that simply there was no need for me to come to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: From what ethnic group did your supervisor belong?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any other Muslim or Croat employees working there on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So did you go home that afternoon or that morning, on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: By the way, were you ever paid for that week's worth of work, where you worked sometimes up to 20 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't pay me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, that afternoon, on the 24th of April, while you were at your apartment, did something happen?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime around 5.00 p.m. they came to my door. It was Naser Cakar, escorted by four or five policemen. They searched my apartment and took me for interrogation to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they seize anything when they searched your apartment?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. It was electrical wiring for a water heater.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they explain why they were searching it? Did they ask you any questions about the electrical wire?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They asked stupid questions, like: Was this wire used to make bombs?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you why you had to go to the police station?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: To give a statement. That's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did they bring you to the police station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you questioned by someone?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who questioned you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Savo Cancarevic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read a section from your statement to move things along a bit, and I'm going to ask you if this was said by him. "At the SUP, I was interrogated by the commander of the police, Savo Cancarevic. He was a Serb. He became a police commander when the war broke out in Bosanski Samac. He asked me all kinds of questions, such as whether I had any weapons, how many Serbs I had killed, how many Serbian children I had slaughtered, and so on." The statement I just read to you, is that a fair and accurate account of the interrogation with Savo Cancarevic?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the date and time when the statement was recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure. I'm sorry. That is from your statement of April 25th and May 3rd of 1998. Your Honour, just for the record, at different points, what I was planning to do, to move things along, rather than spend such as an hour detailing with the witness the beatings that occurred, what I was going to do is just read from his statement and from the interviewing notes, the recent interviewing notes, which have been supplied to Defence counsel, and just ask this witness if those are fair and accurate. Otherwise we'll spend another hour or two going over incident by incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think what you're proposing is better. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you eventually sent to the Territorial Defence building across the street from the police station?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you got to the Territorial Defence building, could you tell us what you saw?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: In the small room, there were about 25 people imprisoned. I can't tell the exact number. I don't know whether there were exactly 25 of them there. All of them were beaten up, bloody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you know these people?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were these people soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were all these people from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, they were not. There were a couple of people who just happened to pass through Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were any of these people wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. None of them had military uniform, but I believe that two people wore police uniforms. I guess that night when the war broke out in Samac, they were in duty, and this is how they were arrested and imprisoned, wearing those police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you were placed in a room with these people?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you under arrest at that time or were you just visiting?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I was under arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you able to leave the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue on during that first night at the Territorial Defence building. Around 10.00, does something happen?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Lugar and several of his cronies, Laki, Avram, people from Serbia, came in and they started firing shots. They got in, and we had to sing Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. What I would like to do now is read basically a summary from your statement of 1998 and your most recent interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, just last week, and I'll ask you at the end if this is an accurate account. And what I'm going to do is read about incidents over the next three days: The 24th, 25th, and 26th. With reference to April 24th, 1992: That same evening I suddenly heard a shot, and at the same time I heard a voice with a Serbian accent. Shortly after the shot, Lugar entered the building, together with Avram and Laki. Avram and Laki are nicknames, and I don't know these men's real names. They were armed with automatic weapons. They were all drunk and they ordered us to sing Chetnik songs. The witness did not know any of these songs and did not want to sing them, but he had to do so. While they were singing, the soldiers went around and beat up prisoners. The witness recalls them hitting Grga Zubak, Sulejman Tihic, and Izet Izetbegovic. Lugar would ask: Who was new? And he would beat the new prisoners. That was the first time that this witness was beaten. This witness was struck only a couple of times that night, and the beating was not that bad. Hasan was shaken and could not believe that this was happening. The beatings continued all night long. It would continue for one half hour, then they would leave, but would return again. Hasan recalls that on one occasion the prisoners had to stand and put their heads down. A soldier would strike them on the back of the head and neck with a long firearm silencer. Mr. Subasic, is that a true and accurate account on what happened on the evening of April 24th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, the basis of the objection is the following: Although we are impressed with this new approach of our learned friend Mr. Weiner to combine various statements, although we don't know exactly which part of which statement he's making reference, we strongly object to this, I would say, hybrid or synthesis of the witness statements, because simply we cannot find many of these details that he is trying to put to the witness. And bottom line of this approach is that it's a kind of mixture of leading questions and some kind of attempts for speculation on the part of the witness. Probably the proper way, according to the well-established practice in these proceedings, might be that our friend first of all will make a reference of exact page, of exact statement, and then read it, put it to the witness, and then same standards should be applied for the proofing notes or -- I don't know how. Or if he cannot establish this way, he can proceed with the examination-in-chief, with a series of questions. Otherwise we are entering into the area which is absolutely unfair for the rights of our clients, and furthermore, it can violate the standards of the fairness of the trial. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully agree with what my colleague Mr. Pantelic has said, and I would just like to note two other things. We here have only one statement from this witness, the statement that was signed, 25th of April and the 3rd of May, 1998. And in the first part of this quote, so to speak, I was able to follow partially this statement, and then the Prosecutor continued reading on things that I do not find in the statement. We were supplied with the notes and the summary by the Prosecutor over the weekend. These are the notes in which the witness describes what happened to him in the third person, and the statement -- this statement is written in the first person. I don't know whether there is any other statement that my colleague from the Prosecution is referring to, or is he reading from the notes and in a way interpreting them? If that is so, then I strenuously object to that practice, because he is merely interpreting the words of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- witness summaries and proofing notes. This is not the first time this problem appears. When we tried as Defence to use proofing notes in cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses, the Prosecution objected and they said these are not the words of the witness; these are just our notes. This is what we heard, but maybe this is not correct or something. So I am strongly opposing of using proofing notes and the witness summaries in the examination-in-chief of a witness. It is all right with the statement that we already have that was signed by the witness, and things like that, but regarding witness summaries and proofing notes, we oppose this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to be sure where you are quoting from. Was it the statement, the proofing notes? What are the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: From my own notes. What I did is I took the proofing notes, from my own proofing notes, and the statement, and I put them all together, rather than go from one to another. Now, we did this previously with one of the protected witnesses, and this was all a result, all a result, of Mr. Pantelic's suggestion that there is no need, that there is no need, to discuss any of the incidents which occurred in the prisons because they have no objection to it. They're agreeing to those things, that those things occurred. Now, he did this again a week or two weeks ago, saying again that they are not fighting that any of these incidents occurred. So what we did, when Witness E testified, we read portions of the statement to move things along. If you would like, I'd be happy to do a direct exam and bring all these details out with the witness. We can take it step by step. I thought that since time was limited, we could do it this way. They opened the issue. We said fine. You're not objecting. They -- Mr. Pantelic said, "We're not even going to cross-examine on these issues." So I figure we can move things along very quickly. However, if the Court would like, I'd be happy to do a direct exam and we'll talk about day by day and go through each of these incidents. I've got no problem with that. I'd be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, well, I can confirm that we took our approach not to have an endless repetition of certain events, but nevertheless it's a matter of fairness and, I would say, to some extent diligence of the parties in these proceedings. Which brings me to another issue: My learned friend should make exact quotes when he quotes the statement of 1998, it should be ERN number, page number, et cetera. And that's the end of story. And then he can say, "Well, now my understanding is of your previous statement, et cetera, that certain events were occurred with the presence of certain persons." That might be done, but we have to clearly divide these issues, Your Honour. It cannot be mixed, you know, in this manner, because otherwise it's not a basis for the defendants. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that as long as the Prosecution indicates where the evidence of the witness has been recorded, whether it's in the proofing notes or in the statement, the Prosecution can take this line of approach. The other point is: These are not contentious matters, the beatings and the ill-treatment that the witness went through, so what has been done so far will remain on record, and the Trial Chamber would like to caution the Prosecution that it's only when it comes to contentious matters that the Prosecution should lead the witness in the normal matters. Otherwise, the objection is partly sustained, but the record will remain as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me continue on. I'll read some from his 1998 statement: "On the 25th of April, Lugar came with his people five or six times to the TO building. He beat us every time he came. I was also beaten by him. I could see that he was drunk again." On the 26th of April --

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: If I may correct you. You said my statement from 1999, and my statement is actually from 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The transcript shows 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The transcript shows 1998. It might have been translated to you as 1999. Either way, I apologise, but it is 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us continue: "On the 26th of April, I saw for the first time one of the local soldiers entering the TO building. This local Serb had joined the White Eagles, which I could see by the insignia on his uniform. His name was Nebojsa, last name unknown, having a nickname of Cera. I knew him from before the war. He beat Omer Nalic and he put a bayonet through his hand. He had a personal revenge against Omer Nalic because Omer Nalic had once refused to hire him in his company. However, he was not only beating Omer Nalic, but the others as well. Members of the White Eagles would also come and take out prisoners, especially the wealthy ones. They would take them to their homes and force them to give them money. Among those taken out by the members of the White Eagles were two brothers Bicic, Hasan and first name unknown, nicknamed Beca." So far, sir, what I've read, is that a true and accurate account of what happened between April 24th and April 26th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me continue with one line, on page 2 of that 1998 statement, and you're talking about Lugar, which is sometime between the 24th and 26th of April: "He put a pistol in my mouth, and when he pulled it out again, he broke two of my front teeth." Did Lugar do that to you sometime between April 24th and April 26th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: From the 24th -- I'm now reading from the Prosecutor's notes, page 2, last paragraph: "From the 24th through the 25th, the men were beaten repeatedly by paramilitaries from Serbia. They were beaten with guns, batons, wooden bats, iron bars, a silencer, a chair/table leg, or whatever else could be found. He describes his first beating on the 24th and having to constantly sing Chetnik songs. He, and when I say he, I'm referring to the witness, recalls details as to who was beaten on various days and the positions they had to maintain as they were beaten. He recalls the cries and screams of the beaten prisoners. What I've read to you so far, sir, is that a true and accurate account of what occurred on those dates, between April 24th and April 26th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, his final statements concern the murder of Dikan, which is -- where there's been already a great deal of testimony. If the Court would like, I would read that information into the record, or we could just move on for the sake of time, since we've already had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we -- yes. We can move on. We have had enough evidence on the matter of Dikan. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we're going to move past the murder of Dikan, because we've already had a great deal of testimony on that issue or on that matter. Now, let us move on. After Dikan was murdered, did any other beatings occur on that day?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ibrahim Salkic was beaten. His nickname was Ibela.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who beat him?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Serbs, Lugar and his people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did Lugar say anything to the rest of you concerning what he was supposed to do with you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he had been given orders - I don't know by whom - to kill all of us who were imprisoned there in the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, later that same day, did something happen, later that evening?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were transferred to Brcko from the TO, to the barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that a military barracks, sir?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long were you and the others held in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I think until the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: About how many people were transferred to the military barracks at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. Some 30-odd people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while at Brcko, were you or any of the other prisoners interrogated?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Superficially by military policemen in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, where were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: In one of the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to read a statement from page 3 of your recent interview with the Office of the Prosecutor: "The witness, or I say he, the witness and some of the prisoners were also interrogated at Brcko. He recalls being questioned there by police. There were two guards standing at his sides, with batons, during the interrogation, which lasted only 15 minutes. He was asked -- or the witness was asked about his military history in Sarajevo in the 1980s. He was not beaten during the questioning." Mr. Subasic, is that a fair and accurate statement concerning your interview at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While at Brcko, sir, did you meet the camp commander there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: At the time it was not a camp; it was simply a barracks of the then still regular Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you held in a barracks room or were you held in a gaol cell at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: In the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while there, did you meet the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came. He introduced himself --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness just said that it was not camp commander. It was not camp. And then in the same question from my learned friend, namely, it's page 59, line 5, and previously he asked also the same thing, the page 58, line 24. I don't think that it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I've got no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. You can deal with that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you meet the barracks commander?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did he say something to you and the other prisoners that were being held there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that they wouldn't beat us there any more, that he knew that we were civilians and had not taken part in any combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were at Brcko, did you see any of the defendants there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was the defendant Simo Zaric doing when you saw him at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I think that on that occasion he came to get three or four prisoners to take them to Samac to be interviewed for television, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the prisoners were who were brought back to Samac to be interviewed by TV Novi Sad, or Serbian television?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that it was Sulejman Tihic, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure about Omer Nalic, although I do believe that he went as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to speak with Sulejman Tihic at Brcko after this television programme?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about the television programme?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I know that he was taken to get a bath, and he put on clean clothes so that he would appear as though nothing had happened to him, and that he had to give the answers that they required him to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you speak with any of the guards? Did you or the other prisoners have the opportunity to speak with any of the guards at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were these guards JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we take a 20-minute break, Mr. Weiner? We shall take a 20-minute break and resume our proceedings at 1750 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Since it is a new moment in our proceedings with this kind of testimony, well, I think whether it's appropriate to have for the record from Madam Registrar in Salt Lake City to know in fact who is present there in the room where the testimony is going, just for the record, to know whether there are some official persons or maybe friends or... Because we are not physically there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, present in the room are the witness, myself, representing the registrar [inaudible] -- something goes wrong with the videolink, he gives us assistance. There's no one else present in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We wish you all the best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And this is a public hearing. So let's proceed, Mr. Weiner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Subasic, let us return to Brcko. When we left, I had asked you if, while at Brcko, you had spoken to some of the guards, and you indicated yes. And the persons who guarded the prisoners at Brcko, were those JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you -- or did they have any discussion with you in relation to Lugar and his paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They said that Lugar and his people came to Brcko several times, but the soldiers did not let them go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you heard this right from the soldiers or the guards?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, from Brcko, where did you go next? You stayed in Brcko maybe a week or less. Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: We were transferred to military barracks in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how long were you in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Until the 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While in Bijeljina, were the prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but not the way we were beaten in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How was it different, sir?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina, they would hit us with fists, whereas in Samac they used anything, any kind of objects to hit us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated you were in Bijeljina until the 13th of May; is that correct, May 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you go on May 13th?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: We were returned to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how were you returned to Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: In a bus. We were returned to the gym of the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any guards on the bus that went from Bijeljina and Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: There were guards, and they were relieved some way half through our trip from Bijeljina to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These guards that went from Bijeljina to halfway along the roadway, did any of them harm or beat the prisoners on that bus?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the guards that took over for the last half of the trip, did they harm or beat any of the prisoners between that last half of the trip to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Not en route; no, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you eventually arrive in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: To the area in front of the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened when the buses arrived at the high school or secondary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They took us out one by one. We got off the bus. And as we would get off the bus, they would start hitting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who would start hitting you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What were they hitting you with?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Rifles, hands, and feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you struck?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Everybody was. All of us prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once they got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. When the witness is talking about local Serbs, were they persons he knew already before, or what is he referring to? It would be interesting to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Subasic, did you hear the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Perhaps you can repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat it for His Honour. His question to you was: When you stated that you were beaten by local Serbs, were you referring to persons that you knew, I assume, who you had seen before, or what did you mean when you said you were beaten by local Serbs? Could you please answer the Judge's question.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I knew those people. I don't know their names, but I know that they were local Serbs from surrounding villages, the villages surrounding Samac. However, I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After you got off the bus and were beaten, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: To the gym of the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, once you got inside of the gym at the secondary school, what, if anything, happened?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: When we got in, we were also beaten by the guards, and also by the guards who had beaten us outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What were you beaten with while inside of the gym?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: With the weapons that they had and with the hands and the feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "with the weapons that they had," could you give us any idea of some of the instruments that they used to beat you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They were mostly armed with Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So when you say they beat you with the weapons that they had, did they hit you with basically the butt of the rifle? Is that what you're indicating?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did they feed you? Did you get any food or drink that night at the high school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry. You don't think so. How long did you remain at the high school or secondary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Only that day and the night following that day, and the next day we were transferred to the gym of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was the elementary school in relation to the high school or secondary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Across the road, about a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you got to the elementary school, where did they place you inside of the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: In the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on that same day, which would be May 14th, 1992, that you were transferred to the elementary school, the elementary or primary school, what happened at the high school or secondary school? Did something happen there? Did someone replace you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: We heard from the guards, and we learned later that this was indeed the truth: Croats had been rounded up and put on trucks. It was some kind of a raid. Men, women, and the elderly were brought into the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were children brought there too?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I think so too. I didn't see any, but I think they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many people were brought to the high school or secondary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I heard that there were 500 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What percentage of these 500 were Croats?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: 99.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you told why these people were sent to the high school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: It was stated that they were in some kind of isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a statement concerning the need for their homes? Was there any discussion concerning that their homes were needed?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Later on, after that, their houses were looted, their property was taken away and stolen, some of their houses were later on inhabited by some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When these Croatian villagers or residents of the municipality of Bosanski Samac were removed from their homes, people of what ethnic group looted their homes?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that people inhabited their homes after they were removed. People of what ethnic group inhabited their homes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek clarification, because I believe that these questions are classic examples of leading questions, because answers are contained in the questions, and because the witness never did say anything about when the houses were inhabited by Serbs, because the chronology is not quite clear in the questions and answers. He was in the prison at the time, and now it is put to him through this question that he knew when it was that these people moved in or moved out from the houses. And I would just like to clarify whether the witness has any knowledge about these facts and where this knowledge comes from, because it's obviously hearsay, secondhand information. Where does this information come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. You should be able to clear that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll be able to clarify it. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's take this one step at a time. Let me ask you about certain facts, and then we'll get to your basis of knowledge, how you know these facts. Let's start off with the homes. People of what ethnic group forced these Croatian villagers out of their homes?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why did the Serbs want these homes to be empty or vacant?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Probably to be able to put their refugees in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have still having the same questions and the same answers. We don't know where does this witness know this, on what basis he knows that, because we know that the witness couldn't see this because he was in prison at the time. So if we are to take this one step at a time, the witness should be asked how he knows that, because now we're in the same situation we were just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. Perhaps you should establish the basis of knowledge for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I just previously said I was going to bring the facts out, then get to the basis of knowledge, but I'd be happy to do it the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While you were held at the primary school, did you have the opportunity, you and the other prisoners, to speak to the guards?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of these guards from the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would they ever discuss what was happening in Samac with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who else did you speak with that provided you with information about what was happening in Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Free civilians or family members, mothers, wives, sisters, they remained in Samac and they were free, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was visitation allowed at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They were not allowed by the police chiefs, but some good guards would allow somebody in at their own risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were any of your family members ever allowed in to meet with you and speak with you at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: My mother was allowed in several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And not only did she speak with you; were they allowed to bring you any food?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did other prisoners also receive visits from their relatives?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as a result of these visits, were you able to learn what was happening in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in addition to these visitors that you and the other prisoners had, did you also receive information from the guards as to what was happening in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did the guards and your visitors, your family visitors, ever discuss the Croats who were rounded up and brought to the high school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They spoke about how they were put in isolation, they were forced to do forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you why these people had to vacate their homes, why these Croats had to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They didn't say anything, but later on, with time, it turned out that Serbian refugees were settled in their houses. This is a fact which is true, and that's how it is to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned isolation. Did the guards have names for the primary school and the high school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They called the secondary school "the isolation", and the elementary school was -- they would say that the extremists were put in the elementary school, things like that. I don't know why, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When the guards referred to the high school or secondary school as "the isolation", where were you being held?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: In the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So the high school was referred to "the isolation" after the Croats were rounded up and placed there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the guards that told you this, or called these locations these names, were they assigned to only one school or to both schools?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They would change places. They would be on guard duty in the secondary school, in the elementary school, in the TO, and in the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could the witness be shown Exhibit P14A, photographs 48 and 49, please. Sir, could you tell us what is depicted in that photograph, number 48?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: This is the picture of the secondary school, and you could see the elementary school in the back, in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So the one in the foreground is the secondary school, the one with the black windows. They look like long black windows in front.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. That's the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the one which is in the middle, where you can only see a portion of the building, that is the --

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: That's the building of -- that's the gym of the elementary school. That's the building that you see in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next photograph, number 49, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what that building is?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Here we see the gym of the elementary school, and we also see the burnt-down building of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So the picture in the foreground is the elementary school. What about those sheds, it looks like, to the left of the elementary school? Is that part of the gym? All the way down at the end of the building.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this is what you're talking about, but that's the burnt-down building of the elementary school. But as I said, I'm not sure what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you for showing the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's return to the primary school. Were prisoners ever beaten at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Every day, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did a day go by while you were at the primary school where beatings did not occur?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How often would he come to the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what would happen when he came to the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: He would always beat up several of us prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would he do that in groups or separately? How would he do it?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Well, when he got in, we had to get up. We slept next to the walls around the gym. And he would go from one to another and beat us. He would beat one person several times, another person just once. He never came in on his own; he had his bodyguards, who were always with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were most of the prisoners beaten by him, or were all of the prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: More or less all of them were beaten by him. He beat some people more severely, others less severely, but practically all of us were beaten by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in June of 1992, there was an incident where your ribs were broken, where you had three ribs broken. Could you tell the Court what happened?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Several soldiers had come. I didn't know them. They beat me up. They ordered me to kneel and to stretch out my arms above my head. And one of them ran up to me and kicked me with his military boot in my right-hand side, breaking my ribs, three of my ribs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Where did this occur? Where in the primary school did this occur?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when they arrived, did you have to sing songs?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had to sing Chetnik songs almost all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you had to kneel and somehow stretch your arms out?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please demonstrate so we could see here how you had to stretch your arms out before they attacked you at your sides?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I had to kneel and stretch out my arms like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that he indicated he had to kneel and he stretched both arms out at a -- I'd say about a hundred-degree angle between his chest and his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you had your arms stretched out, how many people attacked you from the sides?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said that one of them ran to you and kicked you in the ribs?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was he wearing on his feet when he kicked you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Military-style boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as a result, how many of your ribs were broken?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Also during the summer, was there another incident involving your teeth?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. One night soldiers came, and they entered the room. I don't know how many there were, but more than five. They beat people up, taking people out one by one and beating them. Four people held that person down and then they pulled out his teeth with pliers. The rest of us that remained in the gym, 90 or so teeth were pulled from our mouths.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were any of your teeth pulled?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were any others damaged?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. When that person put the pliers into our mouths to pull out one tooth, they would also damage the two adjacent teeth, without actually pulling them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss a few more incidents, or just one more incident at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, these are not contentious issues. It's the details of the beatings and the ill-treatment. Yes. Why don't we move faster, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. One last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have to kneel on a daily basis while at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion we had to kneel for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in which direction did you face while you kneeled for 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Facing the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the guards say anything to you as you kneeled facing the wall during those 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Some would come in, and they would laugh at us. They would say, "Oh, I'm sorry. We didn't know you were praying."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on. The prisoners, these prisoners who were beaten at the primary school, or the prisoners at the primary school, of what ethnic group did they belong?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were these civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you one last photograph, also P14A, photograph 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Actually, it might be better if he could point to certain things on that photograph instead of putting it on the ELMO. It's probably easier if he just points to it, if they can do that from the angle. Could he hold that up for the camera, please? Could he put it in front of him, the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that is, what's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: The gym in the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you lived in that elementary school during the summer of 1992, did you usually stay in one place or location in that gym?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, kind of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you see that spot in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please show the Court.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: This here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So directly under the backboard of the basketball hoop, or a little bit to the right of it as you're facing the photograph?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not directly underneath it, but to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. While you were being held at the primary school, you said you spoke to your family. What was your mother doing at that time? We're talking about during the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: She had to go and do forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did they send her?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: She went to the company called Tekstilac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was she paid for her work?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your uncle, what was your uncle doing?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: My uncle went to dig trenches and perform many other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did your uncle have any children?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: He had a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was Dzevad?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did your uncle and Dzevad both dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was that along the front battle lines, or the front of the battle lines?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they want to dig trenches along the front?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, they did not want to; they had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did something happen to your cousin Dzevad while he was digging trenches along the front lines?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: He was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were either one of them ever paid for their labour?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, they were not, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us move on. Did you ever see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you asked: Did something happen to your cousin Dzevad while he was digging trenches along the front line? Answer: He was killed there. But it's not clear who killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Subasic, were you able to hear the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it. I don't know if the question was addressed to me. I don't know who killed him. I wasn't present. But he was killed there. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did one of the soldiers kill him or was he killed during -- was there fighting going on at the time? Were bullets flying? Were bombs or mortar shells coming down?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The witness answered that he wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. The witness doesn't know. He was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How old was your cousin Dzevad that was killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Weiner. I wonder whether the witness could tell us whether he knows whether the young man's father, who was also digging the trenches, witnessed his son's death.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And secondly, did you ever talk to the father about this at some point when you were able to talk to one another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We talked about that. My uncle lives with me here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where was your uncle when Dzevad died? Where was he in relation to Dzevad?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: According to him, he was there, right next to him, and my cousin died on his arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was trench-digging dangerous along the front lines?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us move on, returning to the primary school, or the elementary school, whatever you'd like to call it. Did you ever see any of the defendants at the elementary or primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who did you see of the defendants at that school during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see Miroslav Tadic at the primary school during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how many times, but every time there was an exchange he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would he come alone or would he come with others?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: He came escorted by the Serbian Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the Serbian Red Cross," is that the local Red Cross from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did you know that they were the Serbian Red Cross from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They had bands with red crosses on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when Miroslav Tadic would come, or when he came in the summer of 1992, did he speak to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I think he did, sometimes, but mostly he came to read out the list of prisoners that were to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, the first time that he came, did he state what his position was in relation to the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He called us Ustashas, balijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is not what he called you, but did he say what his position was in relation to the exchanges? Did he say he worked on the exchanges? Did he say he assisted? Did he say he was in charge of the exchanges? What did he say his position was in relation to the exchange process?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: He said he was in charge of exchanges, and he read out the names of the people who were on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that he would also call the prisoners names, Ustashas and balijas. When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Also there at the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, each time that he came, did he read out names from the list, from these lists of persons to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did he always come with Red Cross officials, local Serbian Red Cross officials?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on those occasions when Miroslav Tadic visited the primary school, how did the prisoners appear? What did you guys -- what did the prisoners look like?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: We were all beaten up, dirty. We had nowhere to take a bath. We were all blue and black. We had blood on our faces, on our clothes. We had lost a lot of weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On those visits, did Miroslav Tadic ever inquire as to your physical condition, either yours or the other prisoners'?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he ever inquire as to the living conditions at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he ever inquire as to the health of any of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These individuals who came from the Red Cross, the local Serbian Red Cross, did they ever make any of those three inquiries as to your health, the physical condition, or the living conditions there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the local Red Cross ever bring any food packages to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they bring any clothing?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Any bedding, meaning pillows, sheets, mattresses?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Never. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about medicine and bandages? Did the local Red Cross ever supply any of that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: The local Red Cross never brought anything, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the local Red Cross ever pass any letters between the prisoners and their families?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any visits from the International Red Crescent Society while at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, not at the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, this is a question for yourself. You mention the International Red Crescent Society. Do I take it that you meant that on purpose? And also you meant not to mention the International Committee of the Red Cross on purpose, or something different?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Something different. Just in case there's any confusion:

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the International Red Cross, or the International Committee of the Red Cross, ever visit you at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that Miroslav Tadic came and read out certain lists of prisoners to be exchanged. After these lists were read by Miroslav Tadic, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: He would go back. I don't know where to, but I know that after that, the people whose names had been called out to be exchanged would always be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So after the names of the prisoners were called out, the prisoners would then be beaten?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would they usually be placed on buses and exchanged immediately thereafter or not, or did it vary from situation to situation?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Well, it varied from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have a question here. Your question was on page 82, line 4: "So after the names of the prisoners were called out, the prisoners would then be beaten?" And the answer is yes. But I would be interested in who was those who beat them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So they would be beaten basically -- I just want to get this right, get this right for the transcript. They would be beaten basically prior to being exchanged, kind of as a final beating, if you want to call it?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, since we're speaking of Miroslav Tadic: While you were at the primary school, did you first hear rumours, any rumours about Miroslav Tadic, while at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I heard that some members of our families - wives, sisters, mothers - went to see him, to see whether he could get any of us exchanged, and he asked them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They asked him how much that would cost and he would give them the prices. I know that because my mother went to see him and to ask him whether he could get me out of the prison and get my wife, myself, and my child exchanged. And he said that would be no problem and would cost 400 German marks per person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So to exchange you, your wife, and your daughter, Miroslav Tadic wanted a total of 1.200 D marks?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, was this during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did your mother know Miroslav Tadic prior to her going to bribe him?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know where she went, where she met with him?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where his office was. I think it was in the vicinity of the pensioners' hall, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did your mother pay him the 1.200 D mark to get you three released?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: She didn't pay him because she didn't have any money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there also an issue in relation to a guarantee if the money was paid?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told her that it didn't depend solely on him, that there were other people who had a say in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So did your mother ever give Miroslav Tadic the 1.200 D-mark bribe that he wanted to have the three of you released?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, she did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you remain in the primary school after that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One last matter in relation to the primary school: While you were being held there during the summer of 1992, were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, once. I was taken from the elementary school to the SUP building, where I gave a statement to a person -- to an inspector who I think was called Milos Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. So you were brought to the SUP. When you were brought to the SUP, what was your physical condition at that time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: All beaten up, black and blue, bloody, dirty, skinny.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do is once again read to you, so we can move along on this, on pages 3 and 4 of your most recent statement and ask you if this is true: "While being held at the primary school, the witness was transported to the SUP to be questioned by Milos Savic. Savic had questioned other prisoners, so the witness had some idea as to what would be asked. He was asked where the defendant was when the war started and on the days that followed. He asked if the witness had a gun. He, Savic, said that he knew everything apparently so you would be candid. The witness was weak, hungry, and tired during the interview. He was beaten recently, he was bruised. At the end of the interview, the witness was given a written statement. He was told to sign it, and did so without reading it. He had no idea what it says." Is that an accurate portrayal of the interview that you had with Milos Savic in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you ever learn what was in that statement, the information that was contained in that statement?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on. Sometime at the end of the summer, were you moved from the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were transferred to the TO building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the TO rooms like when you got back?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: When we got there, we found other imprisoned people from Samac, both Muslims and Catholics. There were perhaps some 60 of them, or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were held at the TO, was anyone beaten?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were the beatings as severe as your first visit to the TO?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No. We got a bit of a break there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the summer, or in the early fall, sometime in the fall, did you ever see Lugar while you were being held at the TO?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did he and his paramilitaries ever visit the prisoners in the TO?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was anyone beaten during those visits?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were those beatings as severe as the initial stay at the TO back in April?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Well, not quite as bad. It was a bit milder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during that time that you stayed in the TO in the late summer and fall of 1992, did the International Red Cross ever visit?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, yes, they did come, but the Serbs closed the door in the TO building where we were and told us that we shouldn't give a peek out, but they took two or three prisoners to the rooms where the guards used. They gave them a bath, gave them good clothing, and they showed them to the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were the Red Cross ever brought into the room where you were being held, you and the other prisoners were being held?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Not while we were there. I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, while you were there, did the guards give you any instructions as to what you could do while the Red Cross was in the other room talking to those two or three show prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said so. They told us we were not allowed to talk amongst ourselves, not allowed to give any sound out, just to be there quiet, and we had to be quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about those prisoners that were placed in the guard room? Were they given any instruction as to what they were supposed to do or so?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: They were given instructions that they were not allowed to say anything about our existence, about the fact that we had been imprisoned, that they had to say that they were there under good conditions, not beaten, that they were simply kept there in order to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were they allowed to say that there were other prisoners elsewhere within the TO facility?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC
utterances.text: No, they were not allowed to say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, it's 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Subasic. We'll continue this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time. The proceedings will begin at 1415 with the other witness, and then 1600 hours we will have the video conference link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 7.01 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of July 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
